prompt: The tempo beat is a quarter note. You change a synced LFO from one cycle per quarter note to one cycle per eighth note at the same tempo. What happens?

options.text: The LFO runs half as fast
options.explanation: An eighth note is shorter, so a cycle takes less time.

options.text: The LFO runs twice as fast
options.explanation: Correct. Two eighth notes fit into one quarter-note beat, so there are twice as many cycles.
Tempo division sets cycle duration; depth is a separate parameter.

options.text: Its phase is guaranteed to align with the next transport beat without any reset policy
options.explanation: Rate synchronisation alone does not establish phase alignment.

workedExample: Keep the beat duration fixed. Fitting two LFO cycles into the time formerly occupied by one doubles the rate. Choose key/transport reset policy separately if cycle starts must line up with notes or beats.

prompt: A tremolo uses a bipolar LFO to move gain above and below unity. Its gain can exceed one while the input already peaks near full scale. What is the problem and the safer range for attenuation-only tremolo?

options.text: No problem; tremolo is supposed to boost and cut equally
options.explanation: A gain above one can push a near-full-scale input beyond the output limit when their peaks coincide. Without coincidence the product of separate maxima is only an upper bound.

options.text: The LFO rate is too slow for tremolo
options.explanation: Rate isn't the issue; the gain range is.

options.text: It can increase peaks and clip; use a unipolar mapping that only reduces gain from unity
options.explanation: Correct. With a unipolar LFO the tremolo only reduces level, never above the original, which is how the lesson's code gave gains between 0.5 and 1.0.

options.text: Bipolar LFOs can't be used for amplitude
options.explanation: They can, if scaled appropriately; the issue is pushing the gain above 1.

workedExample: Check the gain endpoints before checking the LFO rate. A gain above unity can push a near-full-scale sample beyond the output limit when their peaks coincide. An attenuation-only mapping stays at or below unity, so it cannot increase the input’s absolute peak. Depth then determines how far the gain falls.
